technique: the exit — leaving on an image instead of a statement
poem:
Woodsmoke first — somebody's chimney down the valley
already working, that sweet-bitter thread of it
laid over the cold like a hand on the shoulder.
You take it in standing at the sink, the kettle
ticking toward its noise, and let the morning
sort itself the way wet wood sorts fire:
slow, with some stubbornness, some things
that won't catch no matter how you ask them.
Let them be for now. The list keeps.
There's bread going hard on the board, the stove
to feed, the near work and the honest one —
and out past the glass, the hills just coming gray to color.

The day's first light doesn't ask much — just that you meet it, plain and whole, while the house is still quiet enough to hear.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing, the exit. The exit means the poem ends on a thing you can see instead of ending on a statement or a lesson. Look at where this poem leaves you before its final push. Out past the glass, the hills just coming gray to color. That is the last full picture. The poem does not tell you what it means. It just shows you the hills changing color and stops there. This works in a plain way. A statement closes a thought for you. A picture does not. When the poem ends on the hills, you keep looking at them. Your eyes stays on the image after the words end. You feel the morning is still going. Try this. End your poem on one thing a person could point at and cut any sentence after it that explains what it means. The second time through. Listen for how the hills coming to color set up the last line. So up.
